study_context.outcome: Major cardiovascular events (nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, cardiovascular death)
study_context.population: Adults with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk

hypothesis.title: Low potassium and lower resting heart rate identify patients at increased arrhythmic risk from hypoglycemia during intensive therapy
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Difficult samples with lower potassium and lower heart rate reflect either medication effects (diuretics, beta-blockers) or autonomic dysfunction; these patients are more likely to have masked hypoglycemia and be vulnerable to arrhythmia when intensively treated, resulting in higher CV events.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Hypokalemia predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias, and lower heart rate (or concurrent beta-blockade/autonomic neuropathy) can mask adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia, increasing risk of severe outcomes when pursuing intensive glycemic targets.

hypothesis.mechanism: Hypoglycemia triggers sympathetic discharge that, when superimposed on hypokalemia, increases arrhythmogenic potential. Concomitant lower HR (from beta-blockers or autonomic neuropathy) reduces symptomatic detection and timely self-treatment of hypoglycemia, raising the chance that hypoglycemia will precipitate life‑threatening arrhythmias or CV events.
evidence_basis: Physiology: hypokalemia and hypoglycemia both increase arrhythmia risk; beta-blockers/autonomic neuropathy blunt hypoglycemia symptoms
Observed pattern: potassium and heart rate means shifted negative among difficult cases
Clinical reports linking arrhythmic death during hypoglycemia in vulnerable patients
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Patients with potassium <= -0.3 AND hr <= -0.2 assigned to intensive therapy will experience higher rates of severe hypoglycemia-related arrhythmic events and MACE compared with control; removing patients on loop diuretics or with documented autonomic neuropathy will attenuate the interaction.

hypothesis.title: High baseline serum potassium (standardized z >= 0.3) attenuates benefit from intensive glucose control
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: In adults with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, a higher baseline serum potassium (standardized z >= 0.3) is associated with reduced cardiovascular benefit (or comparatively less reduction in major cardiovascular events) from intensive glucose control (HbA1c target <6.0%) versus those with lower potassium.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Higher baseline potassium may mark underlying CKD, RAAS inhibitor use, or predisposition to conduction abnormalities. Intensive glucose lowering often involves greater insulin exposure and risk of glycemia-driven electrolyte shifts; in patients with elevated potassium, this may blunt net cardiovascular benefit or increase risk, so intensive strategy is less likely to be beneficial.

hypothesis.mechanism: Elevated serum potassium frequently reflects reduced renal clearance and/or RAAS blockade; such patients have higher baseline CV risk and are more vulnerable to conduction disturbances. Insulin-mediated shifts in potassium during intensified glycemic control and hypoglycemic episodes may produce unpredictable arrhythmic risk. These factors could reduce or negate the cardiovascular benefit of intensive glycemic lowering.
evidence_basis: Hyperkalaemia is associated with higher mortality and is common in chronic kidney disease and in patients on RAAS inhibitors.
Insulin and acute glycemic shifts alter serum potassium, which can affect cardiac electrophysiology.
Observational studies link electrolyte abnormalities to adverse cardiac outcomes; baseline comorbidity burden (including CKD) modifies effects of cardiovascular interventions.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In an interaction test, the hazard ratio for intensive vs standard glucose control on MACE will be closer to null (or possibly >1) in the subgroup with potassium z >= 0.3 compared with the subgroup with potassium z < 0.3; the treatment-by-potassium interaction term will be statistically significant or show a consistent effect-size difference.

hypothesis.title: Non‑low baseline potassium (standardized z > -0.3) predicts greater benefit from intensive glucose control
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Among the trial population, participants with baseline serum potassium standardized z > -0.3 will derive greater reduction in major cardiovascular events from intensive glucose control (HbA1c target <6.0%) compared with participants with low baseline potassium (z <= -0.3).

subgroup_rule.description: Standardized serum potassium z-score > -0.3 (not in the lower potassium subgroup)

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Patients without low baseline potassium are less likely to experience severe electrolyte-related arrhythmic consequences during episodes of hypoglycemia or insulin-mediated potassium shifts. Therefore the cardiovascular advantages of tighter glycemic control may be realized more fully in this subgroup.

hypothesis.mechanism: Normal-to-higher (but not pathologically high) potassium indicates more stable electrolyte homeostasis and less severe underlying renal dysfunction or diuretic-related depletion. During intensive treatment, these patients should tolerate insulin-related potassium shifts better and have lower arrhythmic susceptibility during hypoglycemia, allowing the atherothrombotic benefits of lower glycemia to translate into fewer major CV events.
evidence_basis: Hypokalemia is linked to increased ventricular arrhythmia risk during hypoglycemic episodes.
Patients with electrolyte depletion or advanced renal disease have higher competing risks that may blunt benefits of preventive interventions.
Prior subgroup analyses in cardiovascular trials often show greater relative benefit of interventions in participants without markers of frailty or advanced organ dysfunction.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: The intensive vs standard treatment hazard ratio for MACE will be more favorable (lower) in the subgroup with potassium z > -0.3 than in the subgroup with potassium z <= -0.3; a treatment-by-potassium interaction (using the > -0.3 cut) will indicate a differential effect consistent with greater benefit in the non‑low group.

hypothesis.title: Older, undertreated patients (no statin/aspirin) have higher harm from intensive control due to frailty/comorbidity
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Older participants who are not receiving statin (and/or aspirin) despite high CV risk represent a frail/undertreated subgroup in whom intensive glycemic control increases adverse events (including CV events) because competing risks and frailty amplify hypoglycemia harms and limit potential benefit.

subgroup_rule.description: Baseline age ≥ +1.0 SD AND statin == 0 (not on statin) and/or aspirin == 0

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Higher chronological age with lack of guideline-directed preventive therapies indicates frailty, multimorbidity, or treatment gaps; hypoglycemia and polypharmacy risks are more harmful than marginal CV gains from tighter glycemic targets in these patients.

hypothesis.mechanism: Frailty and multimorbidity increase vulnerability to hypoglycemia-related falls, arrhythmias, and ischemia. Lack of concurrent evidence-based secondary prevention (statin/aspirin) means the marginal benefit of intensive glycemic control on atherosclerotic events is minimal while harms are amplified.
evidence_basis: Difficult-sample pattern: baseline_age has positive outliers (max 2.49 SD) while statin/aspirin usage not universal (statin mean 0.6, aspirin mean 0.48) in failed cases
Guidelines and trials indicate diminishing returns (and increased harm) of intensive glycemic targets in older/frail patients
Observational evidence that undertreated high-risk individuals derive more benefit from addressing modifiable CV risk factors (statins/antithrombotics) than aggressive glucose lowering
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In patients aged ≥ +1.0 SD and not on statin/aspirin, intensive glycemic control will be associated with higher composite major CV event rates (HR >1.1) and more severe hypoglycemia-related adverse outcomes; initiating statin therapy will reduce overall CV events more than switching to intensive glycemic targets.

hypothesis.title: Younger patients with low atherosclerotic burden derive net CV benefit from intensive glucose lowering
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: In this difficult subset, patients who are relatively younger and have low baseline atherosclerotic burden (no prior CVD, lower LDL) will benefit from intensive glucose control (HbA1c <6.0%) because their cardiovascular risk is more modifiable by metabolic control than by established plaque-related processes that are less responsive to short-term glycemic change.

subgroup_rule.description: Relatively younger (z-score <= -0.2) in this standardized dataset

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Younger patients without prior CVD and with lower LDL are less likely to have fixed plaque burden and more likely to have modifiable metabolic drivers; intensive glycemic lowering can reduce risk mediated by metabolic factors over the trial period.

hypothesis.mechanism: Lower baseline atherosclerotic burden means fewer irreversible plaque-related events. Intensive glycemic control reduces hyperglycemia-driven endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenicity, and pro-inflammatory states that contribute to early CV event reduction in patients whose disease is not dominated by established atherosclerosis.
evidence_basis: ACCORD overall signal that effect differs by baseline risk and prior CVD status
Physiologic evidence that glycemia influences endothelial function, inflammation and thrombosis on a shorter timescale than progression/regression of established plaques
Observed difficult-sample pattern: baseline_age shifted younger (mean negative) and many samples had mixed LDL—defining a low-LDL subgroup isolates those with less plaque burden
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Among patients with baseline_age <= -0.2 AND cvd_hx_baseline == 0 AND ldl <= 0.0, the intensive arm will show lower incidence of MACE over follow-up (relative risk reduction ~ moderate) and not an excess of severe hypoglycemia sufficient to offset CV benefit.

hypothesis.title: Younger patients with isolated hyperglycemia and low antihypertensive burden derive greater benefit from intensive glucose lowering (legacy effect subgroup)
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Younger participants (lower baseline_age) who have pronounced fasting hyperglycemia (high FPG) but relatively few antihypertensive medications (low bp_med) — indicating fewer competing comorbid drivers of CV risk — benefit more from intensive glucose control with lower subsequent MACE risk, reflecting a potential legacy effect.

subgroup_rule.description: Younger standardized age (<= -0.2) combined with metabolic isolation (high FPG and low BP medication burden).

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Younger patients with predominant glycemic pathology and fewer competing vascular comorbidities are more likely to accrue long-term macrovascular benefit from early intensive glycemic control (legacy effect) with acceptable risk profile.

hypothesis.mechanism: Early aggressive control of hyperglycemia in patients with fewer comorbid drivers (lower BP medication burden) mitigates glycation-mediated vascular injury over time, producing delayed but meaningful reductions in macrovascular events.
evidence_basis: UKPDS legacy effect: long-term benefits of early intensive control.
FPG elevation in younger patients may reflect modifiable driver of future CV risk.
Lower comorbidity burden reduces competing risks and therapy complications.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Subjects with baseline_age <= -0.2 AND fpg >= 0.3 AND bp_med <= -0.2 will show a greater relative reduction in MACE over longer follow-up in the intensive arm and fewer early severe adverse events compared with older or multimorbid counterparts.

hypothesis.title: Established CVD and high background secondary prevention (statin/aspirin) modify the relative effect of intensive glycemic control toward neutral or harmful
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: In this set of difficult cases a substantial fraction has prior CVD and high use of statin/aspirin; for these patients, the marginal benefit of further glycemic lowering on cardiovascular outcomes is small and risks (hypoglycemia, weight gain) may predominate, yielding no net benefit or harm.

subgroup_rule.description: Documented prior cardiovascular disease at baseline

treatment_recommendation.rationale: When aggressive secondary prevention (statin/aspirin) is already in place, additional short-term CV risk reduction from intensive glycemic lowering is limited, whereas the risk of hypoglycemia-related adverse events persists.

hypothesis.mechanism: Established atherosclerotic disease results in events driven primarily by plaque instability and thrombosis; these pathways are already targeted by high background use of statins and antiplatelet therapy so that intensive glycemic control contributes little incremental CV protection but still increases hypoglycemia-related risk.
evidence_basis: ACCORD and other trials indicated different responses in patients with prior CVD and the overall excess mortality signal in ACCORD intensive arm
Observed difficult-sample characteristics: cvd_hx_baseline present in ~36% and high statin (76%) and aspirin (56%) use
Mechanistic rationale consistent with additive vs overlapping preventive strategies
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Among patients with cvd_hx_baseline == 1 AND statin == 1, aspirin == 1, intensive treatment will not reduce MACE and may increase mortality; interaction testing will show attenuation of treatment benefit by prior CVD and high secondary prevention use.

hypothesis.title: No prior CVD at baseline — greater relative benefit from intensive glucose lowering
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Participants without documented prior cardiovascular disease at baseline (cvd_hx_baseline == 0) will derive a net cardiovascular benefit from intensive glucose control (HbA1c target <6.0%) relative to standard control, with a lower incidence of major cardiovascular events.

subgroup_rule.description: Patients with no documented history of cardiovascular disease at baseline.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: In patients without prior CVD (primary prevention), intensive glycemic lowering may slow progression of atherosclerosis and reduce first-time major CV events, and these patients may tolerate tighter control with fewer catastrophic hypoglycemia-related complications than those with established CVD.

hypothesis.mechanism: Lowering chronic hyperglycemia in patients without established atherosclerotic disease reduces glycation-driven vascular injury and inflammation, decreasing the likelihood of incident myocardial infarction or stroke; fewer vulnerable plaques and better physiologic reserve reduce hypoglycemia-related adverse consequences.
evidence_basis: Trials of early intensive glycemic control (e.g., UKPDS) showed long-term reductions in macrovascular outcomes when initiated earlier in disease course.
Observational data linking better long-term glycemic control to lower incidence of first cardiovascular events.
Biologic plausibility: less advanced atherosclerosis and better autonomic/cardiorespiratory reserve in primary-prevention populations.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Among participants with cvd_hx_baseline == 0, intensive glucose control will reduce the incidence of major cardiovascular events versus standard control (e.g., hazard ratio ≈ 0.70–0.90; absolute risk reduction detectable within the trial/sample).

hypothesis.title: Any prior CVD (nonzero) — lack of benefit or potential harm from intensive glucose lowering
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Participants with any documented prior cardiovascular disease at baseline (cvd_hx_baseline != 0) will experience no reduction, and possibly an increase, in major cardiovascular events or cardiovascular mortality with intensive glucose control (HbA1c target <6.0%) compared with standard control.

subgroup_rule.description: Patients with any history of cardiovascular disease at baseline (any nonzero indicator).

treatment_recommendation.rationale: In patients with established CVD, intensive glucose lowering may offer limited incremental prevention of recurrent events while increasing the risk of severe hypoglycemia and related cardiovascular complications, tipping the risk–benefit balance away from intensive targets.

hypothesis.mechanism: Established atherosclerotic disease and prior events indicate vulnerable myocardium and plaque burden; severe hypoglycemia induced by intensive therapy can provoke ischemia, arrhythmias, or hemodynamic instability, increasing short-term cardiovascular risk in this high-risk group.
evidence_basis: ACCORD overall findings raised safety concerns about very intensive targets in high-risk populations and observed excess mortality in the intensive arm.
Physiologic and observational data linking hypoglycemia to arrhythmia, myocardial ischemia, and sudden cardiac death particularly in patients with prior CVD.
Secondary analyses of trials indicating differential effects of intensive control by baseline cardiovascular disease status.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: Among participants with cvd_hx_baseline != 0, intensive glucose control will not reduce major cardiovascular event rates and may increase them compared with standard control (e.g., hazard ratio ≥1.1–1.3 for CV events or CV death).

hypothesis.title: High triglycerides (metabolic dyslipidemia) identify insulin-resistant patients who gain less CV benefit and incur more therapy-related harms from intensive control
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Patients with markedly elevated triglycerides or extremes of triglyceride variability represent a metabolically unstable, insulin-resistant phenotype for which intensive fasting glucose lowering increases insulin exposure and hypoglycemia risk without proportionate reduction in CV events.

subgroup_rule.description: Markedly elevated triglycerides (standardized z >= 1.5) or presence of high-outlier TG

treatment_recommendation.rationale: High TGs reflect severe insulin resistance and hepatic dyslipidemia; intensive glucose lowering (especially with insulin) can cause weight gain and hypoglycemia and has limited short-term impact on atherosclerotic risk driven by dyslipidemia.

hypothesis.mechanism: Severe insulin resistance requires larger insulin doses to achieve tight glycemic targets, increasing glycemic variability and hypoglycemia risk; at the same time, atherogenic dyslipidemia (high TG, low HDL) drives CV risk less responsive to short-term glycemic lowering.
evidence_basis: Clinical knowledge linking high TG/atherogenic dyslipidemia to insulin resistance and adverse CV risk that is less sensitive to glycemic changes
Difficult-sample observation: triglycerides showed strong positive skew with high max (outliers)
Trials showing insulin-mediated weight gain and hypoglycemia can offset metabolic benefits
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In patients with trig >= 1.5 (z), the intensive arm will have higher rates of severe hypoglycemia and no significant reduction in MACE; subgroup analysis will show interaction between trig and treatment effect (p-interaction < 0.05).

hypothesis.title: Atherogenic dyslipidemia with absent statin therapy reduces macrovascular benefit of intensive glycemic control
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Participants with high triglycerides, low HDL, and no statin therapy represent an atherogenic, inflammation-driven phenotype in which intensive glycemic control yields little or no reduction in major cardiovascular events compared with standard therapy; resources should instead prioritize lipid-targeted therapy.

subgroup_rule.description: Triglycerides ≥ +1.0 SD AND HDL ≤ -0.5 SD AND statin == 0 (not on statin)

treatment_recommendation.rationale: When residual atherogenic dyslipidemia is dominant and untreated with statin therapy, lowering glucose aggressively is unlikely to materially reduce atherosclerotic CV risk and may expose patients to hypoglycemia-related harms.

hypothesis.mechanism: High triglyceride/low HDL pattern reflects remnant lipoprotein–driven atherosclerosis and systemic inflammation; macrovascular risk in this phenotype is driven primarily by lipid and inflammatory pathways rather than hyperglycemia per se. Intensive glucose lowering reduces microvascular complications more than macrovascular events in such patients; meanwhile hypoglycemia risk remains.
evidence_basis: Difficult-sample pattern: triglyceride distribution includes high outliers (max 3.6 SD); HDL median shifted negative (-0.296 SD), and 40% of difficult samples not on statin
Prior evidence that lipid lowering (statins) produces large macrovascular risk reduction that may dominate glycemic effects
Trial-level meta-analyses showing limited macrovascular benefit of intensive glucose lowering when other risk factors are uncontrolled
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In patients with trig ≥ +1.0 SD, HDL ≤ -0.5 SD and not on statin, intensive vs standard control will show no significant reduction in major CV events (HR near 1.0) and may have higher hypoglycemia rates; initiation of statin therapy will attenuate overall event rates more than switching to intensive glycemic targets.

hypothesis.title: Moderately elevated triglycerides (trig >= +0.5 SD) predict greater benefit from intensive glucose control
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Adults with type 2 diabetes and moderately elevated triglycerides (trig standardized z >= 0.5) will experience a greater relative reduction in major cardiovascular events with intensive glucose control (HbA1c target <6.0%) compared with standard control, compared with participants with lower triglycerides.

subgroup_rule.description: Moderately elevated triglycerides defined as triglyceride z-score >= +0.5

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Moderately elevated triglycerides mark insulin resistance and atherogenic dyslipidemia that may be more responsive to intensive glycemic lowering (which can lower TG and improve lipid metabolism), potentially translating to greater cardiovascular risk reduction in this subgroup.

hypothesis.mechanism: Higher triglycerides reflect hepatic overproduction of VLDL and insulin-resistant lipid metabolism; intensive glycemic control may reduce hepatic TG synthesis and postprandial lipemia, lowering atherogenic particle burden and thus reducing MACE risk preferentially in those with moderate TG elevations.
evidence_basis: Observational links between higher triglycerides and increased cardiovascular risk in T2D
Physiologic association of insulin resistance with elevated TG and impaired lipoprotein metabolism
Prior trials and secondary analyses showing glycemic lowering can favorably modify triglycerides and remnant cholesterol
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the ACCORD dataset, participants with trig z >= 0.5 randomized to intensive vs standard glucose control will have a hazard ratio for major cardiovascular events <1.0 (indicating benefit) and a quantitative interaction between treatment and trig (z) such that the treatment effect is stronger in the >=0.5 group than in the <0.5 group (interaction p < 0.10).

hypothesis.title: Insulin-resistant/metabolic syndrome phenotype (high BMI, high triglycerides, high CPK) has reduced benefit or net harm from intensive glucose lowering
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Participants exhibiting a metabolic syndrome/insulin-resistant profile — elevated BMI, high triglycerides and elevated CPK — do not experience MACE reductions from intensive glycemic lowering and may have net harm because insulin-based intensification increases weight, insulin dosing and hypoglycemia without sufficiently altering the underlying atherogenic milieu.

subgroup_rule.description: Higher standardized BMI (>=0.4) combined with dyslipidemia and muscle enzyme signal.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: This cluster signals insulin resistance with an atherogenic lipid profile; intensive glucose lowering (often with higher insulin exposure) yields weight gain and hypoglycemia without modifying insulin resistance-driven atherosclerotic risk sufficiently.

hypothesis.mechanism: Severe peripheral insulin resistance requires escalating insulin (or insulinogenic agents) to reach low HbA1c, leading to weight gain and more hypoglycemic episodes; persistent dyslipidemia and inflammatory milieu maintain atherogenesis, blunting macrovascular benefit.
evidence_basis: Insulin therapy is associated with weight gain and can increase hypoglycemia risk.
Insulin resistance and atherogenic dyslipidemia drive cardiovascular disease independent of short-term glycemia.
Heterogeneous glycemic intervention effects in patients with metabolic syndrome noted in observational and trial analyses.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the subgroup with bmi >= 0.4 AND trig >= 1.0 AND cpk >= 1.0, intensive therapy will not reduce MACE and will show greater weight gain and hypoglycemia rates compared with control.

hypothesis.title: Low standardized BMI (<= -0.30) predicts harm from intensive glucose control
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Among adults with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, participants with low standardized BMI (<= -0.30) will experience higher rates of major cardiovascular events and/or mortality when randomized to intensive glucose control (HbA1c target <6.0%) compared with standard control.

subgroup_rule.description: Standardized BMI <= -0.30 (lower tail of BMI distribution; lean/frail phenotype).

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Low BMI may indicate frailty, lower metabolic reserve, and greater susceptibility to severe hypoglycaemia and its cardiovascular consequences. Intensive glucose lowering could increase hypoglycaemia-related arrhythmias, falls, and mortality in this subgroup, outweighing potential atherosclerotic benefits.

hypothesis.mechanism: Lean/frail patients have reduced glycogen stores and physiologic reserve and may experience more frequent/severe hypoglycaemia with intensive therapy; hypoglycaemia triggers sympathetic activation, arrhythmia, and pro-thrombotic responses that can precipitate cardiovascular events.
evidence_basis: Observational studies linking low BMI and frailty to increased mortality and vulnerability to hypoglycaemia.
Physiologic data showing greater hypoglycaemia risk and hemodynamic instability in lean/frail individuals on intensive glycaemic therapy.
Prior trial signals (e.g., excess mortality in subsets) suggest heterogeneity of harm with intensive glucose lowering.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the subgroup with standardized BMI <= -0.30, the hazard ratio for the primary MACE outcome comparing intensive vs standard control will be >1.2 (and all-cause mortality will be higher in the intensive arm).

hypothesis.title: Moderately elevated standardized BMI (> 0.20 but below previously-identified high cutoff) predicts relative benefit from intensive glucose control
hypothesis.hypothesis_statement: Participants with moderately elevated standardized BMI (> 0.20 and below the previously implicated high threshold of 0.40) will derive greater reduction in major cardiovascular events from intensive glucose control (HbA1c target <6.0%) compared with standard control.

subgroup_rule.description: Standardized BMI > 0.20 (representing moderate overweight/insulin-resistant phenotype); analysis should exclude those at or above 0.40 to focus on the moderate range.

treatment_recommendation.rationale: Moderately elevated BMI commonly reflects insulin resistance and atherogenic dysmetabolism; these patients may have greater absolute cardiovascular risk driven by hyperglycaemia and therefore could gain more absolute benefit from intensive glycaemic lowering while having lower frailty-related hypoglycaemia risk than lean participants.

hypothesis.mechanism: In insulin-resistant, moderately overweight individuals, tighter glucose control reduces chronic hyperglycaemia-driven vascular injury and may improve lipid and inflammatory profiles, leading to fewer ischemic cardiovascular events; lower frailty mitigates hypoglycaemia-related harms.
evidence_basis: Epidemiologic links between overweight/insulin resistance and higher baseline CVD risk mediated by hyperglycaemia.
Mechanistic studies showing that improved glycaemic control reduces markers of vascular inflammation in insulin-resistant subjects.
Conceptual clinical subgroup findings where benefit from intensive therapy may be greater in higher-risk but non-frail patients.
hypothesis.testable_prediction: In the subgroup with standardized BMI > 0.20 (and < 0.40 when stratified), the hazard ratio for MACE comparing intensive vs standard control will be <0.85, with a greater absolute risk reduction than in lower-BMI subgroups.
